title: Prospective establishment and validation of data-based PET correction methods (motion and attenuation correction) and positronium lifetime at LAFOV PET/CT for children and adults
summary:
Positron emission tomography (PET) measures the three-dimensional distribution of a weakly radioactive substance, known as a 'tracer', which has been injected into the body. This is typically a radioactively labelled sugar variant that accumulates in tumour cells, as well as in areas of inflammation. Other highly specific tracers adapted to respective diseases are also increasingly being used; for example, PSMA-specific tracers are used for prostate cancer.
Images taken in the PET scanner ('tube') provide large amounts of data. This data must first be processed to create a diagnostic image. This involves many steps. For example, errors caused by breathing or organ movement must be corrected ('motion correction'). The properties of different tissues, such as bone, fat, muscle and air in the lungs, must also be considered when creating images ('attenuation correction'). New methods for these correction measurements are constantly being developed and tested in this study. It is expected that new techniques for acquiring and processing PET data sets will contribute to shorter measurement times, lower radiation doses and improved image quality in the future.
conditions: Patients (male, female, diverse), adults, and children who require a PET/CT scan for justified clinical reasons. There may be various clinical indications for PET/CT scans, and various radiotracers may be used.

interventions.name: A clinically indicated standard PET/CT scan is performed first and serves as a control.

First, the clinically indicated standard PET/CT scan is performed (fixed sequence; see arm 1), which serves as a control. Then, in the same patient, additional PET data aquisition are performed after the routine measurements ('arm 2'; this is an intra-individual comparison).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•Age 3 months and older (the planned number of cases is n=40 for children and n=300 for adults),
•Justifiable clinical indication for a PET/CT examination,
•Tolerance of prolonged lying time in the PET/CT scanner,
•Written consent of the patient or legal guardian (if developmentally appropriate, consent of the child).
Exclusion criteria:
•Pregnant or breastfeeding women,
•Claustrophobia or other contraindications for prolonged lying in the scanner, e.g., pain when lying down,
•In case of necessary sedation/anesthesia: contraindications for the study-related prolongation of anesthesia,
•Limited capacity of the patient or legal guardian to give consent.
